title: Strangers
hookLine: a tired stranger on the bus, and metta for the neutral person
tomorrow: a gentle housewife, a maid who tests her, and a kitchen. who snaps?

lines: THE DOORS FOLD OPEN AND SHUT.
cards: On the bus, across the aisle: work boots, a lunch bag on the knees, eyes closed, head tipped against the window. The brakes hiss. The doors fold open and shut.
He doesn't move. Somewhere behind you a phone buzzes, a kid laughs, a bag of groceries tips over and someone catches it. You'll never know his name.
In a few stops he'll get off, and that will be that. So what's his story? Buddhist practice has a name for him, and a surprising job for him in the way loving-kindness is trained.

teach.b: In the Path of Purification, the teacher Buddhaghosa lays out an order for metta. Start with yourself. Then someone dear.
Then the neutral person: someone you neither like nor dislike. Then, later, someone hostile. The neutral person sounds like the easy step.
Often it's the strange one, because there's nothing to push against and nothing to pull toward.
A neutral person is someone the mind has filed away as scenery. The practice un-files them. He stopped being scenery the moment you wondered about his story.
The man on the bus has a whole life: someone who waits for him to get home, a knee that aches on stairs, a worry he took to bed last night, a song he likes.
You don't need to know any of it. You only need to know it's there, as real and as full as yours. The Samyutta Nikaya goes further.
The Buddha says that over the long round of births, it's not easy to find a being who hasn't, at some point, been your mother, your father, your brother, your sister, your son or your daughter.
Some Buddhists take it literally, some as a way of seeing. Hold it loosely or tightly, as you like. Either way, it turns the stranger into family you haven't been introduced to.

how: In loving-kindness meditation, some Buddhist teachers guide people through a sequence that includes a neutral person, such as a shopkeeper or someone passed on the street, before a difficult person.

o: people outside your faith, kept at a polite distance
background figures a calm mind learns to ignore
people with whole lives you'll never see, still worth a wish

games.q: the order of metta — tap the pairs.
p: what the mind does with strangers
hard to find one who wasn't family

s: the neutral person is the easiest step in metta practice
it's often the strange one: nothing to push against, nothing to pull toward.
the Samyutta Nikaya says it's hard to find a being who hasn't been your mother or father
over the long round of births, the Buddha says, such a being is not easy to find.

games.q: the cashier at your grocery store is someone you've seen a hundred times and never really looked at. which move fits today's practice?
o: look up, meet their eyes, and thank them like a person, not a machine.
skip it; metta for strangers only counts in formal meditation.
ask a long list of personal questions to show you really care.
games.why: the practice un-files the neutral person. you don't need their story, only to see that they have one.

practice: Listen for one sound made by someone you'll never meet: a car passing, a voice outside, a door down the hall, footsteps. When it comes, think: they have a whole life. May they be well.
Let the sound fade on its own. Then wait for the next one, and the next stranger.

wordCard.voice: Strangers: the neutral people, filed away as scenery, that metta practice slowly brings back into view.

orig.note: Pali: neutral, standing in the middle; the word for the neutral person in metta practice.

carryVoice: A line to keep: they have a whole life, every one of them. Six of six; friends and community, complete.

sources.ref: Visuddhimagga IX (the order of metta practice: oneself, a dear person, a neutral person, a hostile person)
Samyutta Nikaya 15.14-19 (it is not easy to find a being who has not formerly been one's mother, father, brother, sister, son or daughter)
